author: Thordur Arnason
title: Qwen4-Max Preview is available through Alibaba’s Token Plan
summary: The subscription preview runs through 25 November. Alibaba has posted no pay-as-you-go token price.
paragraphs: Alibaba opened qwen4-max-preview on 11 November at 10:00 UTC+8. The preview ends at midnight UTC+8 after 25 November, and Alibaba says the model will retire then. It is available through Token Plan only.

The international Personal Lite plan lists $6 a month for 20,000 credits. Alibaba limits Personal access to interactive coding and agent tools. Credit use depends on the plan and time of day, so the allowance gives subscribers a budget in credits.
For a metered comparison, the Shortlist still tracks Qwen3.8 Max (0902). Alibaba has yet to publish a pay-as-you-go rate for Qwen4-Max Preview.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Gemini Decision 1 charges for input when scoring predefined choices
summary: Google’s Decisions API can score up to 1,000 questions against shared input, at $0.10 per million input tokens.
paragraphs: Google launched Gemini Decision 1 on 11 November. The Decisions API scores predefined options or criteria against supplied text, images, audio, video or documents. The paid API charges $0.10 per million input tokens and bills no output tokens for the returned scores.

The input meter includes shared material and the tokens used by each question. A request with 50,000 shared input tokens and 1,000 question tokens costs $0.0051. A request can contain up to 1,000 independent questions within the combined limit of 262,144 input tokens.
Budget text generation separately if your workflow also writes a response or explanation.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: NVIDIA’s Kimi K3.1 Pro NVFP4 weights total 1.61 TB
summary: NVIDIA documents eight-way tensor parallelism. Budget separately for the runtime and the KV cache.
paragraphs: NVIDIA’s Kimi K3.1 Pro NVFP4 checkpoint was publicly downloadable when checked on 12 November. Its 96 weight files total 1.61 TB. NVIDIA provides vLLM and SGLang examples using eight-way tensor parallelism and reports testing on GB300.
The file total is a storage figure. Runtime overhead, context length and concurrent requests also affect the GPU memory and throughput your workload needs.
NVIDIA identifies its Open Model Agreement as the governing download terms and links Moonshot’s license for the base model. The Kimi model card separately lists Moonshot’s hosted API rates.
calculatorGuidance: Rent vs Run opens the standard Kimi API quote in custom deployment mode. Enter your measured throughput, utilization and infrastructure costs for the NVIDIA package.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Gemini 4 Carbon opens its paid API at Argon’s rates
summary: Google opened paid API access on 10 November. Standard input, output and implicit cache-read rates double on 1 December.
paragraphs: Google opened Gemini 4 Carbon to paid Gemini API customers on 10 November, following an October rollout to selected users. The API model ID is gemini-4-carbon. Google lists no free API tier.

Direct Standard rates are $2 input, $10 output and $0.10 for implicit cache reads per million tokens through 30 November. From 1 December they rise to $4, $20 and $0.20. Batch, Flex and Priority rates also double.
Argon has the same posted Standard rates. Include thinking in your output budget and compare actual token use and task success on the same workload.

sources.label: Carbon direct rates and serving modes

calculatorGuidance: Choose the same serving plan and workload. Use the scheduled rates for traffic from 1 December, and adjust each model’s token use using your own measurements.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: MiniMax H3-Image API pricing and weight-license limits
summary: MiniMax meters text and images separately. Its 4K promotion ends on 17 November, and its downloadable weights have territorial and commercial limits.
paragraphs: MiniMax announced H3-Image on 11 November. The Standard API charges $2.30 for text input, $1.50 for image input and $3.80 for image output per million tokens. MiniMax’s 4K text-to-image example costs about $0.034 at the promotional rate and $0.069 at list rates. The 50% discount applies to outputs of at least 16.6 million pixels and ends at 16:00 UTC on 17 November.

MiniMax lists a 68.65 GB checkpoint and a separate 66.7 GB text encoder. Its community weight license excludes the EU, UK, South Korea and US. It requires prior written authorization for third-party hosting or annualized revenue above $1 million.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview Qianfan prices and weight access
summary: Baidu publishes peak and off-peak rates in yuan. The separately downloadable Flash Base checkpoint has its own license.
paragraphs: Baidu’s 10 November Qianfan rate card lists promotional peak rates of ¥1 input, ¥4 output and ¥0.10 cached input per million tokens from 08:00 to 22:00. From 22:00 to 08:00 they fall to ¥0.50, ¥2 and ¥0.05. List rates are twice those amounts. The promotion page gives 23:59:59 on 30 November as the end time, with the timezone unspecified.
The earlier OpenRouter quote was $0.28 input and $1.13 output per million tokens. On 12 November the route returned no active endpoints. Baidu still listed direct Qianfan access.

Baidu published the separate Flash Base checkpoint on 5 November under a custom license. Baidu says it plans to release Flash Preview weights under Apache 2.0. The exact Preview download remained unverified on 12 November.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Claude Fable 5.2 lowers standard token rates
summary: Standard input and output rates fall 20% from Fable 5.1. Anthropic applies 30-day data retention unless it expressly authorizes an exception.
paragraphs: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on 9 November. Standard direct rates are $8 input and $40 output per million tokens, down from $10 and $50 on Fable 5.1. Cache reads cost $0.20 per million. Batch costs $4 input and $20 output. The optional Fast mode costs $16 and $80.

Fable 5.2 is available to Claude API customers. The accompanying Mythos 5.2 release is restricted to verified organizations. Both require 30-day data retention unless Anthropic expressly authorizes zero data retention.
Fable 5.1 remains active while teams test the migration. Check your own token mix and re-run workload evaluations before estimating savings.
calculatorGuidance: Use the same workload for both Standard plans, then adjust token volumes and cache assumptions using your own measurements.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Muse Ember triples direct rates above 200,000 input tokens
summary: Meta applies the long-context rates to the whole request. Cached input and restored conversation history count toward the threshold.
paragraphs: Meta released Muse Ember on 9 November at $0.10 input, $0.004 cached input and $0.50 output per million tokens on its direct API. Above 200,000 input tokens, the entire request is billed at $0.30 input, $0.012 cached input and $1.50 output per million.

Cached input and restored conversation history count toward the threshold. A request with 210,000 uncached input tokens and 10,000 output tokens costs $0.078 before tools. At the headline rates it would cost $0.026.
The Tape quotes OpenRouter’s Muse Ember route. Check the terms for the route you use before budgeting a long prompt.
calculatorTitle: Compare Muse Ember’s two direct tiers
calculatorGuidance: Choose Standard through 200,000 input tokens and Standard long context for larger requests. Enter the full input count before setting the cache-hit percentage.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: LongCat 2.5 weight downloads range from 1.34 TB to 3.56 TB
summary: Meituan publishes two MIT-licensed checkpoints. ZenMux lists a separate promotional API quote.
paragraphs: Meituan announced LongCat 2.5 on 2 November. By 10 November its publisher repositories listed two public MIT-licensed checkpoints. The main checkpoint contains about 3.56 TB of weight shards and the W4A4 package about 1.34 TB.
Those totals cover the weight files alone. Use Rent vs Run to budget for the hardware, runtime memory and utilization of your chosen serving setup.

For a hosted comparison, ZenMux listed promotional rates of $0.30 input, $0.006 cached input and $1.18 output per million tokens when checked. The corresponding regular rates were $0.75, $0.015 and $2.95. Check the current ZenMux quote before budgeting.

updates.text: showed general availability on 7 November. Direct rates held at $0.70 input and $2.10 output per million tokens. Mercury 2, 2.5 and 3 lost their OpenRouter listings by 8 November. Inception still posts direct Mercury 3 prices.

Neither download was verified at cutoff. Deep Principle announced Hydrogen-1.0 and lists a hosted route, while its exact weight repository requires approval.

takeaways.title: Match the bill to the workload
takeaways.text: Video output, decision input and text completion use different meters. Check the endpoint and unit before entering a rate.

takeaways.text: A public checkpoint still comes with license terms and a hardware bill. Model files give you a starting point for sizing memory.

coverage: This is a selection of verified events. Some publisher sources and gated artifacts were inaccessible.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: P-H3-Image ComfyUI memory and weight-license limits
summary: Pruna publishes image generation and editing weights with a measured 21 GB memory example and geographic limits on use.
paragraphs: Pruna released P-H3-Image on 3 November with downloadable weights for image generation and editing. Its 4-bit ComfyUI configuration lists about 20 GB of downloads. Pruna reports 21 GB peak VRAM at 8 megapixels for the diffusion model, text encoder and VAE. Budget separately for the prompt upsampler.

The bundled MiniMax H3 Community License excludes the EU, UK, South Korea and US. The agreement points users in those territories to MiniMax for separate licensing. If the terms cover your use, take the measured setup as a starting point for estimating hardware and running costs.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash change models and rates on 1 December
summary: Google will reroute two legacy Gemini API IDs to different models on 1 December. Check the replacement rates and request parameters before the switch.
paragraphs: On 2 November, Google announced that direct Gemini API requests to gemini-2.5-pro will serve Gemini 3.8 Flash from 1 December. Requests to gemini-2.5-flash will serve Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. Google will bill each at the replacement model’s rates.

For December, Google lists Standard rates of $0.75 input and $3.75 output per million tokens for 3.8 Flash, and $0.30 input and $2.50 output for 3.5 Flash-Lite. Google schedules 3.8 Flash to rise to $1.50 input and $7.50 output on 1 January. Test the replacement model against your own requests, especially thinking settings and tool calls. Check separate routed offers with the service you use.

The Marginal Token’s automated Google check is using its last verified prices after Google moved the pricing page to AI Studio. On 4 November we compared all five cached Google rates with the official Standard price rows and confirmed they match.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Claude Opus 5.5 message threads shrink requests while billing stays the same
summary: Anthropic’s Messages API beta lets clients send only the new turn. The server rebuilds the conversation, and prompt caching remains a separate setting.
paragraphs: Anthropic’s 2 November message threads beta lets agents using Claude Opus 5.5 and other Claude models send only the new turn. Anthropic reconstructs the conversation on the server and says pricing and rate limits stay the same.
Configure prompt caching separately. When estimating costs, use the input, cache read, cache write and output counts reported by the API. Request size alone misses the history the server restores.
A thread expires after five idle minutes, so keep the history needed to replay the conversation. The beta is ineligible for zero data retention and HIPAA use.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: GLM 5.3 FlashX Legal direct and routed prices
summary: Z.ai and OpenRouter list the same token rates for FlashX Legal. Each service uses its own model ID and documents its own hosting and cache terms.
paragraphs: OpenRouter lists GLM 5.3 FlashX Legal from 2 November under z-ai/glm-5.3-flashx-legal. Z.ai documents the direct API ID glm-5.3-flashx-legal separately. Use the ID for the service you call.

Both services list $0.37 for uncached input, $0.075 for cache reads and $1.25 for output per million tokens. Z.ai lists direct cache storage as free for a limited time. OpenRouter lists the route without EU in-region hosting. Check the applicable terms on the service you plan to use.
Our model card records the OpenRouter quote. For a direct estimate, use Z.ai’s listed rates in the workload calculator.

takeaways.title: Measure accepted work
takeaways.text: Terra and Particle’s efficiency claims are vendor results. Compare retries, reasoning, cache hits and review time on your own tasks.

takeaways.title: Budget the complete deployment
takeaways.text: OCR and speech weights need memory, serving software and operating effort. Review license conditions before counting infrastructure savings.

updates.title: First-party access and prices
updates.text: Mistral Medium 3.5/Large 3 were deprecated on 31 October. Kimi K2 closed to new API users; full retirement is planned by end-December. Independent routes remain separately sourced.

updates.title: Endpoint and tool charges
updates.text: OpenAI FedRAMP adds 10% from 1 November. DeepSeek’s stated server-side Search/Fetch billing start has passed: $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests, additional to tokens.

updates.title: Serving and regional availability
updates.text: Gemini Computer Use reached GA. QwenCloud added GLM 5.3 US access. Ollama 0.40.13 lists LFM3 audio/omni support on Linux and Windows.

updates.text: Mage-VL-Cowork, LBS-27B, Ling-3.1-flash-1019 and Youtu-Parsing-Omni are accessible checkpoints. Observation dates are not release dates; Youtu’s license includes an EU territorial condition.

watching.text: Gemini Carbon and Genie 4 have restricted previews; MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash serves verified MDASH customers. Cadence Maestro targets selected early-access customers. None establishes general public API access.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Surya 2.5: local OCR costs and commercial-license limits
summary: Datalab’s OCR weights are public. Their commercial terms differ from the Apache-licensed code, and measured pages per second depend on the serving setup.
paragraphs: Datalab released Surya 2.5 on 29 October with public OCR weights. The code is Apache 2.0; the weights use modified AI Pubs Open Rail-M terms.

The weight license restricts use by entities above $5 million in prior-year gross revenue or total equity/debt funding, with personal/research exceptions. A separate restriction covers products or services competing with Datalab or its affiliates. Broader licensing requires separate terms. Read the exact license for your deployment.

Datalab reports faster processing on tested H100 and Apple Silicon setups. Those are vendor measurements at specified resolutions and concurrency. Budget rendering, inference, retries and review, then compare cost per accepted page. Rent vs Run helps estimate infrastructure costs; licensing can add a separate bill.

title: GPT-6 Rosalind Research: posted prices, restricted access
summary: OpenAI’s life-sciences model has a public rate card and restricted Research access. Discovery approval and ChatGPT subscriptions do not establish access or API billing eligibility.
paragraphs: OpenAI announced GPT-6 Rosalind Research on 30 October, using API ID gpt-6-rosalind. It is rolling out in Work, Codex and the API to approved organizations and authorized users for internal research. It is not available in the Chat tab. Discovery approval does not grant Research access.

Standard short-context API rates are $15 input, $1.50 cached input and $75 output per million tokens. Long-context rates and cache-write charges differ. A published rate card is not general availability, and subscription allowances are a separate offer.

Enterprise access starts with a two-week Admin Preview, off by default. Existing GPT-5.5 Rosalind Research remains available; Discovery stays on 5.5. Budget the actual tariff, repeated runs and qualified review time. The workload calculator supports explicit rate overrides; it does not determine model eligibility.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Youtu-Parsing-Omni: public weights, deployment costs and license limits
summary: Tencent’s 5B parser has public weights and a serving plugin. Its custom license includes an EU territorial limitation; checkpoint size alone does not establish running costs.
paragraphs: Tencent’s Youtu-Parsing-Omni is a 5B-class model that parses documents, images, audio and video into structured JSON. We verified its public checkpoint, serving plugin and inference examples on 31 October. The publisher’s README dates the release only to October; repository creation is not a public-availability date.

Its License Terms of Youtu-Parsing include an additional territorial limitation stating that the model is not intended for use within the European Union. The terms cover inference code, parameters and weights. Check the exact license for your deployment.

The documented vLLM recipe uses BF16, 65,536-token context and one concurrent sequence, with separate pinned environments for vLLM and Transformers. It does not establish a universal GPU-memory minimum or a hosted API price. Use Rent vs Run, then measure throughput and review effort per accepted document or media job. Benchmark scores are publisher results.

NVIDIA’s headline throughput comes from optimized NIM serving with NVFP4 and DFlash2. The model card says those serving optimizations are not yet in the open-source release.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Particle-1: token savings and the serving plan behind the bill
summary: Particle’s coding model has distinct direct peak, off-peak and Flex rates. Vendor task-cost comparisons assume high cache reuse; steering can leave more than one generation billable.
calculatorTitle: Compare Particle-1 and Terra on your workload
calculatorGuidance: Select the direct peak/off-peak and eligible Flex plan that matches your requests. The schedule follows America/New_York and is locked per request. Routed quotes have their own terms. Use observed cache hits, count reasoning once within total output, and include original hidden tails, steering successors, retries and tool fees.
paragraphs: Particle launched Particle-1 on 28 October, post-trained from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for coding. Its current direct peak prices are $0.25 input, $0.03 cached input and $1 output per million tokens, including reasoning.

Direct off-peak rates are half price from 20:30 to 04:00 America/New_York. Eligible Flex requests receive another 50% token discount. Those direct billing rules must not be assumed for an OpenRouter quote.

Particle’s reported task-cost savings use vendor benchmarks, assumed tariffs and a fixed 95% cache-hit rate. They are not a guaranteed saving on your workload. Mid-turn steering can also leave the original generation running privately and billably; a missing immediate usage figure does not mean zero cost.
Compare all generations, retries and accepted outcomes in the workload calculator, using the actual serving plan and observed cache hits.

title: LFM3: local deployment and the commercial-license threshold
summary: Liquid’s downloadable models have a custom commercial license and separate runtime memory costs. Its text API now lists $0.08 input/$0.20 output per million tokens, with $0.02 cached input.
paragraphs: Liquid AI announced LFM3 on 27 October, with public weights spanning text, vision, audio, omni and decision models. The text checkpoint, LFM3-1.7B, supports 256K context. Liquid estimates about 1 GB at four-bit precision; runtime and long-context memory still need a separate budget.

The weights use the custom LFM Open License v1.0, with a $10 million annual-revenue threshold and a definition of legal entity that includes controlled affiliates. Larger businesses need a separate agreement for commercial use. Check the full terms when assessing eligibility.

Use Rent vs Run to budget deployment, then measure throughput, completed tasks, memory and engineering time on your own workload. Liquid’s launch benchmarks are vendor results.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Qwen Audio 3.1 Realtime Flash: four billing meters for voice
summary: QwenCloud’s new voice model bills text and audio separately. International and mainland China tariffs differ; token prices alone do not establish a cost per minute.
paragraphs: QwenCloud added qwen-audio-3.1-realtime-flash on 27 October. The real-time speech model accepts and returns text and audio, with function calling and voice cloning.

The International tariff separates four meters: $0.23 per million text-input tokens, $0.93 per million audio-input tokens, $0.70 per million text-output tokens and $1.87 per million audio-output tokens. Mainland China has a separate tariff. These are token rates, not prices per minute.
Budget the actual text and audio usage returned by the API, alongside any separately charged tools or voice services. A text-only comparison omits part of a voice application’s bill.

The guide lists retained audio-history limits of 50 turns and 300 seconds, with 20 turns retained by default. These are history limits, not a five-minute call cap; earlier history is discarded. The release entry separately lists a 262,144-token context window. Measure cost per completed conversation before replacing an existing voice stack.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: GPT-6.1 Terra: token prices, long prompts and the routed Pro variant
summary: OpenAI’s new model costs $1 input/$5 output per million tokens at Standard rates up to 272,000 prompt tokens. Longer prompts and cache retention change the bill; OpenRouter’s Pro route uses the same underlying model.
calculatorTitle: Compare Terra and Sol on your workload

paragraphs: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on 26 October at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens. Cached reads cost $0.05. Above 272,000 prompt tokens, the full request uses $2 input and $7.50 output rates, with higher cache rates too. Tool calling requires the Responses API.

Standard cache writes cost $1.25 per million tokens for 30-minute retention or $2.50 for 12 hours. Batch and Flex have lower published rates; Fast is a separate serving mode. Regional processing adds 10% where available, and tool charges are additional.

OpenRouter describes “Terra Pro” as the same underlying model with a different reasoning mode. It is a routed serving variant, not evidence of a separate OpenAI model release. More reasoning can increase tokens per completed task despite identical token prices.
Compare representative completed tasks, retries and review effort. OpenAI’s performance and task-cost comparisons are vendor results. Sol remains our basket selection.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Unlimited-OCR-2: measure the cost per accepted page
summary: Baidu’s public OCR weights target long-document parsing. Runtime, throughput, reprocessing and review determine running costs; its published 80GB test GPU is not a stated minimum.
paragraphs: Baidu’s 27 October announcement brings public Unlimited-OCR-2 weights and code for long-document parsing; the checkpoint was uploaded on 26 October. The model card labels the weights MIT, and the code repository publishes MIT terms. Its fixed-reference attention is a design for bounding attention work, not proof of a constant total document bill.

Baidu documents Transformers and SGLang serving. The published Transformers test used an A800 with 80GB memory; that is a tested setup, not a stated minimum. Hardware, throughput and accuracy need measurement on the documents you actually process.

Budget capacity, then measure cost per accepted page—including reprocessing and human review. Baidu’s benchmark results and efficiency claims have not been independently replicated here. No paid API tariff has been verified for this exact release.

The separate MarathonDocBench repository provides evaluation annotations and page images. Its Apache-2.0 metadata applies to that evaluation release; it does not establish that the model’s training data is public.

paragraphs: This edition covers Monday 19 to Sunday 25 October, with access and pricing updated through today’s Kimi and MiniMax Market Notes. Announcement dates, checkpoint uploads and our verification dates are kept distinct.

The week brought cheaper frontier API access, local coding and conversational models, and specialists for decisions, extraction and speech. The practical question is which offer fits the job, including its billing units, license and operating requirements.

updates.text: Nanbeige4.3-33B has a 24 October checkpoint upload, Apache-2.0 metadata and 512K context. Carbon-X’s 22 October checkpoint combines DNA and language under Apache-2.0; use its supported tokenizer/runtime. Ling-3.0-flash-Sante has MIT-labelled healthcare research weights, with no exact release day verified. No clinical validation is inferred.

updates.text: NVIDIA’s RFD4-Proteina bundle and Cosmos3 Nano-Sim checkpoints extend biology and simulation tooling. Retrieval weights, Hy-Memory GGUF and INCO’s Qwen drafter packages are distinct from new base-model launches. Seedance Pro Fast is documented on Volcano Ark; fal’s FLUX 3 Max video offer lists promotional per-second pricing. Exact first-access dates for these offers remain unverified.

Standard Pro cache hits cost $0.20 per million tokens. Cache writes cost $2 for 5-minute retention or $4 for 1 hour; hits refresh the selected period without another write charge. Allocate input to uncached tokens, reads or writes once. Compare accepted task cost on your own workload.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Flint: local coding, hardware requirements and running costs
summary: Recursive’s coding model has downloadable Apache-2.0 weights. Its optimized Mac runtime requires specific chips and at least 48 GB of memory; running costs depend on hardware use and task success.
paragraphs: Recursive released Flint on 21 October, with Apache-2.0 weights for a coding model containing 39.8 billion parameters, roughly 2.5 billion active per token. It is designed to investigate codebases, fix bugs and implement features.

Recursive’s optimized rec runtime requires an M4 Pro, M5 Pro or M5 Max Mac with at least 48 GB of unified memory. Other runtimes have separate requirements. NVIDIA deployments are available through vLLM and SGLang; NVIDIA RTX Spark support for rec is still described as coming soon.

Local execution avoids API token charges, but hardware, electricity and setup still cost money. Recursive’s speed and coding scores are vendor claims. Test representative tasks on your intended runtime, including retries and review time. Compare cost per accepted code change, with realistic assumptions about how often the machine will be used.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Clairic: extraction at $0.10 per million input tokens
summary: Cloudflare’s extraction preview charges for input only. The practical test is cost per accepted extraction, including validation and human review.
paragraphs: An invoice number, a delivery date or a receipt total is a small job to give a general-purpose language model. Cloudflare’s Clairic offers a specialist alternative: define the fields you need and receive typed values, with confidence scores for extracted answers and intervals for estimates.

Released on 19 October as a Workers AI preview, Clairic is available through the @cf/cloudflare/clairic endpoint. The posted rate is $0.10 per million input tokens, with no output-token charge. It accepts text and up to four images. Check the API’s reported usage when budgeting: field definitions contribute tokens, and requests can span multiple processing passes.

The economics are promising for repetitive document work, but a correctly formatted answer can still be wrong. Cloudflare describes limitations in multi-step arithmetic and forecasting, and says uncertainty intervals can be too narrow on unfamiliar data. Extract the facts, use code for calculations and test review thresholds on representative documents. Cloudflare’s performance claims still need validation on your workload.
Open weights are planned; the announcement makes the hosted preview available now. Treat self-hosting as a future option until downloadable weights and license terms are available.

The useful comparison is cost per accepted extraction. Count the model call, retries, validation and human review against your current pipeline. A lower token bill matters most when it also reduces the cost of getting a correct result.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Mercury 3: launch prices and the Mercury 2 migration deadline
summary: OpenRouter’s Mercury routes have ended. Inception still posts direct Mercury 3 pricing, with separate access terms for older models.
paragraphs: Mercury 3 launched on 19 October at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens, half its regular $0.20/$0.70 rates. Cached input costs $0.01 per million tokens during the offer. No promotion end date is stated on the checked pricing pages.

Inception has also closed Mercury 2 and 2.5 to new direct customers. Customers with usage before 19 October retain access until 15 November; enterprise agreements are treated separately. That is Inception’s policy, not a confirmed shutdown of every third-party route.
Budget against both tariffs and test migration before the deadline.
Update, 9 November. OpenRouter listed 8 November as the expiry date for Mercury 2, 2.5 and 3. Those routes have since disappeared from its model catalog and their endpoint lists are empty.

Inception still lists the direct API model mercury-3 at $0.10 input, $0.01 cached input and $0.35 output per million tokens under its launch offer. Regular rates are $0.20, $0.02 and $0.70, respectively. A workload with one million uncached input tokens and one million output tokens costs $0.45 at the posted promotional rates or $0.90 at regular rates.

author: Thordur Arnason
title: Haiku 5.5: higher API rates above 100,000 prompt tokens
summary: The 100,000-token boundary changes both input and output rates. Price agent workloads by prompt length, with cached tokens included.
paragraphs: Haiku 5.5’s standard API rate starts at $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens. Above that threshold, the rates rise to $0.50 input and $2.50 output.

Anthropic counts cached reads and cache writes toward a request’s prompt length. Each request is priced individually, so a cache hit can reduce billable cost while the prompt still crosses into the higher tariff.
For long conversations and agent runs, context management changes the tariff as well as the number of billable tokens. A one-million-token context window comes with more than one price band.
